content: Maternal hypotension is the most common complication associated with spinal anaesthesia during caesarean sections. This condition can lead to symptoms such as nausea and vomiting and may result in severe consequences for both the mother, such as unconsciousness and pulmonary aspiration, and the baby, including hypoxia, acidosis, and potential neurological injury. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various prophylactic interventions aimed at preventing hypotension following spinal anaesthesia in women undergoing caesarean sections. The review included 125 randomized controlled trials involving 9,469 women. These studies focused exclusively on interventions to prevent maternal hypotension and excluded any active treatments for hypotension. The primary outcomes assessed were the incidence of hypotension requiring intervention and neonatal Apgar scores of less than 8 at five minutes. No studies reported neonatal intensive care unit admissions. Crystalloid versus no fluids: The administration of crystalloids reduced the incidence of maternal hypotension compared to no fluids (average risk ratio [RR] 0.84, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72 to 0.98; 370 women; 5 studies; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference between the groups in terms of nausea and vomiting (average RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.91; 1 study; 69 women; very low-quality evidence). No neonates in either group had an Apgar score of less than 8 at five minutes (60 babies; low-quality evidence). Colloid versus crystalloid: Colloids were more effective than crystalloids in reducing the incidence of maternal hypotension (average RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.81; 2009 women; 27 studies; very low-quality evidence). However, there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of maternal hypertension requiring intervention, bradycardia requiring intervention, nausea and/or vomiting, neonatal acidosis, or Apgar scores of less than 8 at five minutes. The evidence for these outcomes was of very low quality. Ephedrine versus phenylephrine: There was no significant difference between ephedrine and phenylephrine in preventing maternal hypotension (average RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.18; 401 women; 8 studies; very low-quality evidence) or hypertension (average RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.71 to 4.16; 2 studies; 118 women; low-quality evidence). However, the incidence of bradycardia was lower in the ephedrine group (average RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.64; 5 studies; 304 women; low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in nausea and/or vomiting, neonatal acidosis, or Apgar scores of less than 8 at five minutes. Ondansetron versus control (placebo): Ondansetron was more effective than placebo in preventing hypotension requiring treatment (average RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.83; 740 women; 8 studies; low-quality evidence), bradycardia requiring treatment (average RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.87; 740 women; 8 studies; low-quality evidence), and nausea and/or vomiting (average RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.51; 653 women; 7 studies; low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in neonatal acidosis or Apgar scores of less than 8 at five minutes. Lower limb compression versus control: Lower limb compression was more effective than control in preventing hypotension (average RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.78; 11 studies; 705 women; very low-quality evidence). There were no significant differences in bradycardia or nausea and/or vomiting. No neonates in either group had an Apgar score of less than 8 at five minutes. Walking versus lying: There was no significant difference between walking and lying in terms of hypotension requiring treatment (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.21; 1 study; 37 women; very low-quality evidence). The quality of evidence across the studies was generally low to very low, primarily due to limitations in study design, imprecision, and indirectness. Most studies included only women scheduled for elective caesarean sections, which limits the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, the use of colloids should be approached with caution due to the potential for serious adverse effects, such as allergic reactions and renal failure. In conclusion, while interventions such as crystalloids, colloids, ephedrine, phenylephrine, ondansetron, and lower limb compression can reduce the incidence of maternal hypotension, none of these methods completely eliminate the need for treatment in some women. Furthermore, the evidence is insufficient to draw conclusions about rare adverse effects associated with these interventions.
